# Red-Team: Chained-Root Append-Only Ledger on a Git Bus

## Core invariant being attacked

Every defense reduces to four conjuncts that must hold simultaneously:

> **head_root = F(all entries) ∧ head_root is fresh ∧ head_root is unique ∧ head_root is anchored outside the mutable store**

Each bypass below targets exactly one conjunct. A mitigation is "deterministic" here in the strict sense: it compiles to a mechanical accept/reject predicate with no judgment call.

---

## 1. Force-push history rewrite

**Bypass:** `git push --force` (or `git update-ref`) replaces the bus tip with a rebuilt chain. Because the attacker controls the whole repo, they recompute every downstream `prev_root` cheaply — internal hash-chain validity survives a full rewrite.
**Fix:** Two layers, both mandatory. (a) Mechanical append-only at the transport: `git config receive.denyNonFastForwards true` plus a `pre-receive` hook asserting `newtip.first_parent_chain` extends the current tip. (b) External anchor: witness set records `(height, root)` tuples outside the repo. Verifier predicate: `∀ (h, r) ∈ anchor_log : chain[h].root == r`. Layer (a) stops accidents and outsiders; layer (b) stops anyone holding the repo.

## 2. Genesis forgery / parallel universe

**Bypass:** Build a complete ledger from a fabricated genesis declaring whatever initial state the attacker wants. Every internal hash verifies.
**Failure it exploits:** nothing pins the starting point.
**Fix:** Hardcode `GENESIS_ROOT` as a constant in every verifier build. Predicate: `entry[0].prev_root == GENESIS_ROOT`, checked before anything else. Mismatch → reject entire presentation, no further parsing.

## 3. Tail truncation (silent rollback)

**Bypass:** Drop the last *k* entries. The remaining prefix is perfectly self-consistent — truncation is invisible to purely structural validation.
**Failure it exploits:** no freshness binding.
**Fix:** Witness quorum periodically signs checkpoints `(height, root)`. Acceptance predicate: `head.height ≥ last_certified.height ∧ certified_root is reachable in chain(head)`. Anything shorter than the last certified height is rejected outright — not flagged, rejected.

## 4. Equivocation (forked views)

**Bypass:** Serve victim A a chain forked at height *h*, victim B a different fork from the same ancestor. Both are internally valid; each victim sees a consistent world.
**Fix:** Witnesses countersign **exactly one** root per height (threshold/BLS multisig). Any two valid quorum certificates `(h, r₁ ≠ r₂)` constitute *fork evidence*: both are published to the dispute log automatically, and the treaty treats fork evidence as an unconditional halt-and-alarm condition. Client-side predicate: refuse any head lacking a quorum certificate, and gossip every received head so divergence surfaces with probability → 1.

## 5. Chaining bypass / splicing

**Bypass:** Insert an entry omitting or corrupting the `prev_root` field, betting on sampled verification; or reorder entries inside a batch, exploiting that a batch-level Merkle root may not commit to intra-batch order.
**Fix:** (a) Verification is *total, never sampled*: recompute `rᵢ = H(domain ‖ canon(entryᵢ) ‖ r_{i-1})` for every entry in any presented range; first mismatch rejects the whole presentation. (b) Canonical deterministic encoding (fixed-width integers, explicit lengths, sorted fields — CBOR canonical form works) so any permutation changes the hash. Schema violations are decode failures, which are rejections.

## 6. Hash downgrade / collision injection

**Bypass:** If anything in the pipeline still speaks SHA-1 (legacy git objects!), chosen-prefix collisions are economically feasible today: mint two entries with identical object IDs — benign twin shown to auditors, malicious twin actually applied.
**Fix:** Pinned algorithm allowlist in the treaty spec: SHA-256 minimum everywhere. Repos initialized `--object-format=sha256`; packs containing any SHA-1 object rejected at receive. Domain-separate the root function (`H("leaf"‖x)` vs `H("node"‖l‖r)`) to kill second-preimage and extension ambiguities. Spec version is itself committed as entry zero-adjacent metadata, so downgrades show up as rewrites.

## 7. Checkpoint-gap exploitation

**Bypass:** Strike inside the window between two signature checkpoints; when challenged, present the pre-checkpoint prefix (valid) and bury the tail.
**Fix:** Continuity predicate: for consecutive certifications `cᵢ, cᵢ₊₁`, require `cᵢ₊₁.height − cᵢ.height ≤ K` (treaty max interval), and require the head to carry a certificate or sit within one interval `K` of the last one — heads older than `K` past the last certification are never auto-trusted, only served with an explicit "unverified tail" flag that downstream consumers treat as rejection.

## 8. Timestamp forgery

**Bypass:** Git committer dates are freely settable (`GIT_COMMITTER_DATE`). Forge timestamps to make a truncated or forked ledger look current and defeat staleness heuristics.
**Fix:** Ledger-internal timestamps are *informational only, load-bearing nowhere*. Freshness derives exclusively from witness attestations, each carrying RFC 3161 tokens or the witness's own signed clock reading. Verifier compares attestation time against local clock with bounded skew for alarms. Deterministic because the trust input is a signature, not a string in the repo.

## 9. Signer-host compromise (rewrite + re-anchor)

**Bypass:** Compromise the box holding the signing key and the repo; rewrite history *and* issue valid-looking new checkpoints. Structural checks and single-sig checks both pass.
**Fix:** Quorum certificates from *t+1-of-n* witnesses with HSM-held, operationally independent keys. Rotation and revocation events are themselves ledger entries at height *R*; certificates from keys revoked at ≤ *R* are invalid thereafter. Under this regime a successful rewrite requires forging a threshold — cryptographically excluded — or colluding a quorum, which is outside the threat model by declaration. Partial compromise manifests as conflicting certificates, i.e., item 4's fork evidence fires.

## 10. Cross-ledger replay / namespace confusion

**Bypass:** Copy signature-valid entries from ledger A into structurally identical ledger B, or replay old entries after a rollback attempt.
**Fix:** Every signature payload binds `(ledger_id ≔ genesis_hash, height, root, entry_hash)`. Verifier predicate: `sig.ledger_id == own_genesis`, else reject. Height uniqueness (one entry per height) enforced in the receive hook, killing intra-ledger replay.

## 11. Git-layer grafting: merges, cherry-picks, side refs

**Bypass:** Push a merge commit grafting foreign history onto the bus branch (DAG looks plausible), or publish tampered history on a side ref (`refs/heads/bus-audit-mirror`) and socially point clients at it.
**Fix:** Hook on the single canonical ref `refs/heads/bus`: (a) fast-forward only; (b) each new commit has exactly one parent equal to the previous tip — merges are structurally impossible on this ref; (c) commit body parses to schema-valid entry; (d) declared root equals recomputed root; (e) push signature valid (`git push --signed`). All other refs are *unprotected but untrusted*: verifiers consume only `refs/heads/bus` from a pinned remote URL over pinned SSH/HTTPS. Side-ref content has zero evidentiary weight by construction.

## 12. Object-store tricks: `git replace`, alternates, shallow clones

**Bypass:** `git replace` transparently swaps an object's content behind an unchanged ID; `objects/info/alternates` points audits at a doctored store; shallow clones hide depth and let a truncated history masquerade as complete.
**Fix:** Audit procedure is fixed and non-negotiable: run with `GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1`; reject any clone dir containing `alternates` or `.git/shallow`; require a full clone; then **independently recompute** every object ID and every root from raw objects. Terminal predicate: `recomputed_head == claimed_head`, byte-exact.

## 13. Inclusion-proof shortcutting

**Bypass:** Hand auditors a syntactically valid Merkle inclusion proof terminating in a root the attacker invented, counting on them to verify the proof but not question the root.
**Fix:** Single rule, no exceptions: **no proof is accepted unless its terminal root equals a quorum-certified, externally anchored root.** Auditors check proofs against the certified-root map, never against repo-declared roots.

## 14. Adjacent: append-griefing (integrity-adjacent availability)

Not tampering, but it degrades the same invariant: sybil floods inflate the ledger, forcing auditors toward sampled (i.e., bypassable) verification. Fix: signed-push certificates, per-committer rate limits, hard entry-size cap in the receive hook — keeping total verification (item 5a) affordable forever.

---

## Residual risk boundary (what this design honestly does not cover)

1. **Full quorum collusion** — by definition outside the model; the design converts it from silent forgery into visible fork evidence only if even one honest witness persists.
2. **Verifiers who don't verify** — tamper-evidence is not tamper-*awareness*; a fork wins against any party that skips the predicates above. The mitigations are deterministic only when executed.
3. **Bootstrap window** — the span between genesis and the first external anchor supports an undetectable rewrite. Close it with a multi-party genesis anchoring ceremony at time zero.

Everything else in the attack surface above maps to a mechanical check, and every check maps to a reject path.
reasoning:
The user asks me to red-team a tamper-evident append-only ledger where every entry commits to the prior root, in the context of a "Ghost-AOS git-bus treaty." This is a hypothetical system — I need to be concrete and grounded. Let me reason about what this architecture is:

- Append-only ledger: entries can only be added, never modified or deleted.
- Each entry commits to the prior root: so entry N contains (or commits to) the Merkle root of the ledger state after entry N-1. This creates a hash chain of roots — a blockchain-like structure.
- "Git-bus treaty": presumably a protocol where git commits act as a message bus, with a treaty/spec defining how parties agree on the ledger. Git itself provides content-addressed storage (SHA-1/SHA-256 object hashes), append-only-ish refs (refs move forward but can be force-moved), signed tags, etc.

So the threat model: an adversary wants to rewrite history, insert fake entries, fork history, suppress entries, roll back state, etc., while evading detection by the tamper-evidence mechanisms.

I need to enumerate bypass attempts and deterministic mitigations for each. Deterministic mitigation = a concrete, mechanical defense, not "be careful."

Let me systematically enumerate attack classes:

**1. History rewrite via ref manipulation**
- Attack: `git push --force` / `git update-ref -d` + re-push rewritten history where old commits are re-created with same messages but different content, then new entries appended. Since each entry commits to prior root, the attacker must also recompute all subsequent roots — which is feasible if they control the whole repo and hashes are cheap.
- Why it might work: git refs are mutable pointers; force-push replaces branch tips. The commit chain integrity alone doesn't stop rewriting if you rebuild the whole chain from genesis.
- Deterministic mitigation: anchors external to the mutable repo. Signed root checkpoints published to a transparency log / witnessed by multiple parties; or anchor the genesis and periodic roots in an immutable store (e.g., another git repo treated as read-only via signed tags, or an external append-only log like Rekor/Trillian). Every root at height h must be verifiable against a witness set threshold. Also: hooks on receive (`pre-receive` hook rejecting non-fast-forward updates) makes the bus append-only mechanically. Both together: fast-forward enforcement locally + external anchoring for compromise scenarios.

**2. Genesis forgery / alternate universe**
- Attack: attacker builds a complete parallel ledger from a forged genesis block that claims some initial state, then presents it as the real ledger. All internal hashes check out.
- Mitigation: pinned genesis commitment — every verifier hardcodes the expected genesis hash (root_0). Any ledger whose first entry doesn't match the pinned constant is rejected. Deterministic: constant comparison.

**3. Entry omission / truncation (rollback without rewrite)**
- Attack: truncate the tail — drop last k entries. Remaining prefix is fully valid internally. E.g., revert to an earlier state to hide a transaction.
- Mitigation: freshness checks — witnesses/signators sign "latest observed root at time T"; verifiers require the head root to be at least as recent as a quorum-signed checkpoint. Monotonic sequence numbers + signed head announcements. Deterministic rule: accept only heads ≥ latest signed checkpoint from witness quorum; any head below that is rejected outright.

**4. Forking (equivocation)**
- Attack: present different valid ledgers to different victims (split view). Each fork is internally consistent because forks diverge from a common ancestor and each side appends its own entries committing to shared ancestor root.
- Mitigation: gossiped uniqueness — every entry includes the previous root; two distinct heads claiming the same height h with different roots = fork proof. Deterministic: any party observing two signed heads at the same height publishes both; the treaty defines fork evidence as automatically disqualifying/requiring investigation, plus witness quorum must sign exactly one root per height. Require cosigning: each entry's root must be countersigned by ≥ t-of-n witnesses; witnesses refuse to sign two roots at same height, making forks cryptographically evident (like key-transparency / CONIKS-style).

**5. Root-commit bypass (splicing)**
- Attack: insert an entry that does NOT commit to the prior root — i.e., skip the chaining field, hoping validators don't check. Or reorder sibling entries within a batch since batch-level root may hide intra-batch order.
- Mitigation: strict schema validation — decoding rule rejects any entry missing/mismatched prev_root; verification is total, not sampled: verify(root_{i} == H(entry_i || root_{i-1})) for all i in any presented range. For intra-batch ordering: include per-entry index and canonical serialization (deterministic encoding, e.g., sorted keys, fixed-length fields) so any permutation changes the hash. Deterministic: canonical encoding + total chain verification.

**6. Hash-collision / downgrade attacks**
- Attack: exploit weak hash (SHA-1 collision — git historically SHA-1). Attacker crafts two entries with same hash: benign one shown to auditors, malicious one actually applied. Chosen-prefix collisions on SHA-1 are practical (~cost).
- Mitigation: mandate SHA-256 (or SHA3-256/BLAKE3) everywhere — objects, root computation, signatures domain separation; reject SHA-1 objects entirely (GIT_DEFAULT_HASH=sha256, reject legacy object formats); length-prefix + domain separation in the root computation (H("leaf" || bytes) vs H("node" || l || r)) to prevent second-preimage/extension ambiguities. Deterministic: algorithm allowlist pinned in the treaty spec version.

**7. Signature stripping / unsigned gap exploitation**
- Attack: find a window between signature checkpoints and push malicious entries there; when auditors check, attacker shows pre-checkpoint prefix (valid) and hides tail; or relies on lazy verification.
- Mitigation: continuous notarization — every Nth entry (or every entry) is cosigned; verification requires unbroken signature coverage: no gap larger than the treaty's checkpoint interval; a head without a valid cosignature chain back to the last anchored root is rejected. Deterministic: coverage check over [anchor_height, head].

**8. Metadata/timestamp manipulation**
- Attack: forge timestamps to make a truncated/forked ledger look current, defeating staleness detection. Git committer dates are trivially settable.
- Mitigation: don't trust embedded timestamps for freshness; rely on signed witness attestations with externally-verifiable time (witnesses use their own clocks / signed timestamp services — RFC 3161 TSA). Deterministic: freshness = f(quorum attestation), not ledger-internal time.

**9. Insider/host compromise — rewrite + re-anchor**
- Attack: attacker compromises the machine holding the signing key and the repo; rewrites history AND signs new checkpoints. Internal consistency + valid signatures.
- Mitigation: threshold signatures / multi-party witnesses with keys held separately (HSMs, independent operators); key rotation with revocation published in the ledger itself; any rewrite implies either (a) colluding quorum — out of model — or (b) detectable via dual-signature evidence (two conflicting quorum certificates at same height). Deterministic: quorum certificate requirement + automatic fork-evidence alarm on conflict.

**10. Replay across ledgers / namespace confusion**
- Attack: take valid entries (with signatures) from ledger A and inject into ledger B (same format), or replay an old entry after rollback to re-validate stale state.
- Mitigation: bind signatures to ledger identity: every signed structure includes ledger_id (genesis hash) and monotonically increasing height; verifiers check sig covers (ledger_id, height, root). Replay within a ledger blocked by height uniqueness enforced at receive hook. Deterministic: domain-separated signature payloads.

**11. Merge/pull abuse in git layer**
- Attack: use merge commits to graft foreign history into the bus branch, creating a DAG that superficially looks fine; or cherry-pick entries out of order; or push to a side ref that auditors don't watch while clients get pointed at it.
- Mitigation: bus branch accepts only linear first-parent chains (pre-receive hook: verify each new commit's parent == previous tip and that commit content matches the entry schema and recomputed root); single canonical ref (refs/heads/bus) protected; all other refs ignored by verifiers; clients pin the ref name + fetch from allowlisted remotes over authenticated transport. Deterministic hook logic.

**12. Object-level tampering outside refs (dangling objects, alternates, replace refs)**
- Attack: `git replace` to swap an object's content transparently; or manipulate alternates file to point at a doctored object store; or shallow clones hiding depth.
- Mitivation: disable replace refs in verification context (`GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1` / config `core.useReplaceRefs=false`); verify full closure: recompute every object hash in presented range and recompute roots from raw objects; forbid alternates/shallow in auditor procedure; verify pack integrity. Deterministic: audit runs with replace off + full-hash walk.

**13. Denial-of-append / griefing (not tampering but availability attack on append-only property)** — maybe out of scope; the ask is tamper-evidence bypass. I could mention briefly: sybil pushes to inflate ledger; mitigation: write capability ACL + rate limits. Keep short or omit. I'll mention briefly as adjacent.

**14. Compact-range proof forgery / audit shortcut abuse**
- Attack: present a Merkle inclusion proof that's valid-looking but for a doctored tree; auditors verifying only proofs, not the chain of roots.
- Mitigation: proofs must resolve to a root that is itself anchored (quorum-certified). Rule: no acceptance of any proof terminating in a non-anchored root. Deterministic.

Also worth structuring: the core invariant is "head_root = F(all entries) ∧ head_root is fresh ∧ unique ∧ anchored." Each attack targets one conjunct:
- Rewrite → breaks anchoredness
- Fork → breaks uniqueness
- Truncation → breaks freshness
- Splice → breaks F
- Collision → breaks F's collision-resistance assumption
- Key compromise → breaks anchoredness unless threshold

Let me make sure each mitigation is genuinely deterministic (mechanical predicate):

1. Force-push/rewrite → denyNonFastForwards=true + pre-receive hook verifying first-parent lineage from current tip; PLUS external anchor: root_h recorded in witness log; any presented history must contain the anchored root at height h with matching value. Predicate: ∀ anchored (h, r): ledger[h].root == r.

2. Genesis forgery → hardcoded GENESIS_ROOT constant in verifier binary/config; reject otherwise. Predicate: entry[0].prev_root == GENESIS_ROOT.

3. Truncation → monotonic signed checkpoints: witness quorum signs (height, root) periodically; verifier requires head_height ≥ last_certified_height and head chain reaches certified root. Predicate: head.height ≥ C.height ∧ path(C.root) ∈ chain(head).

4. Equivocation/fork → witnesses sign one root per height under BLS/threshold; two certs at same height with different roots = fork proof, auto-quarantine + alarm. Predicate: ∄ two valid quorum certs (h, r₁≠r₂) accepted ever.

5. Chaining bypass/splice → total verification: recompute rᵢ = H(dom || encode(entryᵢ) || r_{i-1}) for every entry in range; canonical CBOR/RLP encoding with fixed-width integers and explicit lengths. Reject on first mismatch. No sampling.

6. Collision/downgrade → SHA-256 minimum; reject sha1 object format (init with --object-format=sha256; verify pack uses sha256); domain-separated hashing: leaf vs node prefixes prevent cross-type second preimages.

7. Checkpoint-gap exploitation → signature coverage continuity: for consecutive certified heights c_i, c_{i+1}, require c_{i+1}.height − c_i.height ≤ K (treaty max interval) and each intermediate root derivable; head must carry cert or fall within one interval of last cert with pending-witness status (never auto-trust beyond K).

8. Timestamp forgery → freshness derived solely from quorum attestations; ledger timestamps informational only; witnesses attach RFC 3161 tokens or their own signed time. Verifier compares against local clock ± skew bound for staleness alarms.

9. Signer compromise → n-of-t threshold certs (t+1 independent holders, HSM-backed); rotation entries committed in-ledger; old key revoked at height R — certs signed by revoked keys invalid after R. Compromise ⇒ attacker must forge threshold ⇒ detects as inability; partial compromise yields conflicting certs = fork evidence.

10. Cross-ledger replay/copy-paste → sig payload binds (ledger_id := genesis_hash, height, root, entry_hash). Verifier rejects sigs whose ledger_id ≠ own genesis. Height uniqueness enforced by hook (one entry per height).

11. Git-layer grafting/merges/side-refs → pre-receive on refs/heads/bus: (a) update is fast-forward; (b) each new commit has exactly one parent == previous tip; (c) commit body parses to schema-valid entry; (d) recomputed root matches declared root; (e) signature valid. All other refs unprotected-but-untrusted: verifiers only consume refs/heads/bus from pinned remote URL + SSH known_hosts / HTTPS pinning.

12. Replace refs / alternates / shallow → auditors run with GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1, forbid .git/objects/info/alternates in audit image, require full clone (reject shallow), and independently recompute every object ID + all roots from objects rather than trusting reported values. Predicate: recomputed_head == claimed_head.

13. Inclusion-proof shortcut → rule: proofs only trusted if terminal root equals an anchored/quorum-certified root; else reject. Auditors verify against certified root map, not repo-stated roots.

14. DoS/griefing (adjacent): push ACL (signed push certs, `git push --signed`), rate limit, entry size cap in hook. One line.

Residual risk statement: what's NOT covered — collusion of quorum, client-side verification refusal (people who don't check), and post-compromise rewrite before first external anchor (bootstrap window) → mitigate with genesis-time multi-party anchoring ceremony. That's honest grounding.
